SEC16A-01.note: Either/or: verb agrees with the nearer subject (nestmates, plural); 'Ever since' + ongoing study requires present perfect. A tempts by agreeing with 'a lone scout'; C/D are tense foils that 'Ever since' rules out.

SEC16A-02.note: Inverted clause after 'Only in...': subject is the singular 'assumption', and 'decades since' running to the present needs present perfect 'has ... begun'. B tempts via the plural nouns 'decades/submersibles/vents' directly before the blank; D fails with participle 'begun' but that word is far from the blank.

SEC16A-03.note: Relative clause verb agrees with antecedent 'shoots' (plural) and must be passive (the shoots were preserved). A is attractive because the main subject 'revival' is singular and 'is remarkable' follows; B is the plural active foil.

SEC16A-04.note: Delayed compound subject after 'there' (both X and Y) is plural; past narrative keeps simple past. A tempts via 'there was' habit and the singular 'glue/binder' near the blank; B/D shift to present perfect in a past narrative.

SEC16A-05.note: Inverted past counterfactual 'Had ... not taken' requires 'would have been' in the result clause. A (mixed conditional) is the strongest foil but the past-time 'could then be seen' rules out a present result.

SEC16A-06.note: Third member of a series of simple-past verbs (drifted, lingered, and headed). C tempts via 'only after ... had begun', but the past perfect belongs to the subordinate clause, not the series.

SEC16A-07.note: List items containing internal commas (appositives) are separated by semicolons. A is the commonest foil (all commas makes 'a dairy culture' read as a fourth item); B repeats colons after the sentence's own colon and C runs items together, both strikable on sight.

SEC16A-08.note: The engraver made more than a dozen plates, so the title restricts 'plate' and takes no comma before it. C tempts strongly because the printed comma after the title looks like the close of a pair; the key leaves a comma before 'because', which is acceptable but may make some readers doubt B. D's dash-comma mismatch can be struck on sight.

SEC16B-01.note: Subject 'mortar' is singular despite the 'including ... fragments' interrupter, and the verb takes the object 'the hairline cracks', so it must be active. C tempts via 'fragments'; D is singular but passive, which leaves the delayed object with no role.

SEC16B-02.note: A fraction of a mass noun ('two-thirds of the buried carbon') is singular, and the carbon was carried in, so the verb is passive. B tempts via 'two-thirds' and 'cores'; C/A are active forms that make the carbon the agent.

SEC16B-03.note: When 'each' follows a plural subject ('The two notebooks ... each'), the verb stays plural; the notebooks are digitized by volunteers (passive). B is the strong foil because 'each' immediately before the blank reads as a singular subject; C/D are active.

SEC16B-04.note: A present participial phrase gives the result of 'breaks ... and carves'. A is a finite verb after a comma with no conjunction and a tense shift; D's perfect participle wrongly places the leaving before the carving.

SEC16B-05.note: Reported future after the past 'assured' takes future-in-the-past 'would'. B echoes the engineer's direct words and is the main foil, but the prediction has already turned out false, so it cannot stay in 'will'; D's past perfect places the keeping before the assurance.

SEC16B-06.note: The age is what gets determined (passive), and the general claim takes the modal 'can'. A tempts as the matching modal but makes the age the agent; C is passive but in the wrong tense.

SEC16B-07.note: A colon after a complete clause introduces the noun phrase that specifies 'a feature'. A puts a fragment after a semicolon; C is the closest foil, since a sentence-final appositive set off by a comma would attach to 'magnification', not to 'feature'; D can be struck on sight.

SEC16B-08.note: A list with no verb is summed up by 'any one of these conditions'; the dash marks that summary. A leaves the list as a verbless fragment; B is the strongest foil (a comma is weaker and nonstandard for a resumptive summary); D can be struck on sight.

tells: Comma never wins any of the four punctuation items: it is a foil in A-07 (A), A-08 (C), B-07 (C) and B-08 (B). A test-taker who rejects the plain comma option is never penalized.

Strong-mark key: in three of four punctuation items the key is the heaviest specialized mark (A-07 semicolons, B-07 colon, B-08 dash). The one exception, A-08, keys the no-mark option, so the heuristic 'avoid the comma' still holds.

Passive wins whenever voice varies across the options: A-03 (D), B-02 (D), B-03 (A) and B-06 (D) all key the passive form. Only B-01 keys active against a passive foil, so 'pick the been/being option' scores 4 of 5.
The would-forms win both modal-tense items (A-05 'would have been', B-05 'would keep out').
The no-punctuation option (B-07 D, B-08 D) is always ungrammatical in isolation and can be struck free.
Key letters are balanced: A4 B4 C4 D4.
